edges.description: Type I interferon is a central driver of lupus autoimmunity.

Central nervous system inflammation, including vasculitis, is frequent in patients with an interferon signature; the causal route from interferon to vascular inflammation is not established.
Seizures are the commonest neuropsychiatric presentation of the central nervous system inflammation that accompanies the interferon signature; the causal route is not established.
Loss of tolerance manifests as SLE or an SLE-like illness in most patients.

nodes.description: Biallelic variants in C1QA, C1QB or C1QC either abolish C1q (nonsense, splice, start-codon and some missense variants that prevent assembly or secretion) or yield a low-molecular-weight C1q that circulates at low level but is not functional. Loss of a single chain is enough to prevent C1q production even when the other two chains are made.

nodes.description: Because C1q is made by monocyte-derived cells, allogeneic HSCT restores C1q production and classical pathway function and can cure the disease. In a multicentre series of 18 patients transplanted mainly for refractory autoimmunity, autoimmune features resolved in 11, but five died of transplant-related complications and survival was worst in patients with renal or neurological involvement, so patient selection is critical.

evidence.reference_title: Hematopoietic Stem Cell Transplantation for C1q Deficiency: A Study on Behalf of the EBMT Inborn Errors Working Party.
evidence.snippet: In eleven patients HSCT led to resolution of autoimmune features and discontinuation of immunosuppressive treatments (follow-up time range 3-84 months). Five patients died due to transplant-related complications.

evidence.reference_title: Allogeneic Hematopoietic Stem Cell Transplantation in the Treatment of Human C1q Deficiency: The Karolinska Experience.
evidence.snippet: A 9-year-old boy and a 12-year-old girl with refractory SLE restored C1q production after allo-HSCT. This resulted in normal functional properties of the classical complement pathway followed by reduced severity of SLE symptoms.

nodes.description: C1q binds apoptotic cells and, with the early classical pathway components, promotes their removal by macrophages. In C1q-deficient mice apoptotic bodies accumulate in glomeruli and are cleared poorly from the peritoneum. This is the basis of the waste-disposal hypothesis, in which persisting apoptotic material supplies the nuclear autoantigens of SLE. The defect has been demonstrated in mice rather than measured directly in patients.

nodes.description: SLE or an SLE-like illness develops in most patients, usually in early childhood. In a 2015 literature review 55% of 71 reported patients met ACR criteria for SLE and a further 22.5% had an SLE-like syndrome; an international follow-up survey of 45 patients found SLE in 80%. Compared with sporadic SLE, discoid rash and oral ulcers are more common and arthritis and anti-dsDNA antibodies less common.
